title: Mechanism for the diluent response in asthma.
abstract: To investigate the mechanism underlying the airway response to diluent challenge, three adult asthmatic patients who were known to be reactive to inhaled diluent were studied. Airway response as measured by conventional pulmonary function testing was measured under the conditions of time, inhalation of room air, diluent and placebo. Two of the patients responded to time or to room air, suggesting that the response was not due to the phenol-buffered diluent. The third subject reacted primarily to the diluent and not to time, room air or normal saline. Two of the three patients were placebo responders.

screening.rationale: Small within-subject controlled case series that explicitly investigated airway responses to diluent/placebo and identified placebo responders, so placebo/diluent response was the object of study.

classification.summary: Studied three adult asthmatic patients' airway responses to time, room air, diluent and placebo and found heterogeneous responses, with two patients showing placebo-type responses.
classification.key_finding: Two of three patients showed airway responses to time or room air rather than the diluent, and two were identified as placebo responders.

title: Active and placebo effects in treatment of moderate and severe insomnia.
journal: Journal of consulting and clinical psychology

screening.rationale: Title indicates an empirical study of active and placebo effects in insomnia but no abstract or full text was available to confirm study design, outcomes, or whether placebo/nocebo was a primary focus.

classification.summary: Title indicated an empirical trial comparing active and placebo treatments for moderate to severe insomnia, but no abstract was available to confirm methods or results.

title: Visual evoked potentials as a predictor of reported side effects during a trial of zimelidine vs. placebo in chronic pain patients.
abstract: Before a double-blind controlled study of zimelidine, a new, rather specific inhibitor of serotonin uptake, in patients with chronic pain, visual evoked potentials (EPs) to stimuli of varying intensities were recorded. During the trial the blood levels of zimelidine and its active metabolite norzimelidine were estimated. Side effects were rated by a physician before and after the trial. No significant difference in frequency of side effects could be found between the zimelidine and the placebo groups. Furthermore, there was no significant relationship between the blood levels of the active drug or its metabolite and the frequency of side effects. Instead, a significant relationship was found in the total group between the frequency of side effects and the tendency to react with an increase in maximum amplitude of the EP when stimulus intensity was increased (i.e., augmenting). The same trend was clear both in the zimelidine group and in the placebo group. Thus the augmenting/reducing response in visual EPs seems to be a predictor of the side effects reported irrespective of the drugs given.

screening.rationale: Empirical double-blind trial that analyzed predictors of reported side effects across drug and placebo groups, i.e., nocebo/placebo-related responses.

classification.summary: Recorded visual evoked potentials before a double-blind zimelidine vs placebo trial and found that an augmenting VEP pattern predicted higher frequency of reported side effects across both drug and placebo groups.
classification.key_finding: Augmenting increases in maximum visual evoked potential amplitude with stimulus intensity predicted greater side-effect reporting irrespective of zimelidine or placebo assignment.

title: Placebo effect and changes in response set with re-testing: a further source of bias.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH indicate the paper addresses placebo effects and methodological bias in response sets, making placebo science/methodology the main subject despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Discusses how placebo effects and changes in response set with retesting can introduce bias in studies and the methodological implications for research design.

title: Effect of transdermally administered scopolamine in preventing motion sickness.
abstract: The efficacy of transdermally administered scopolamine was compared with the efficacy of oral dimenhydrinate and placebo therapy in the prevention of motion-induced mausea in a vertical oscillator; medications were administered on a double-blind cross-over basis, with the order of treatments counterbalanced. Thirty-five subjects known to be susceptible to the stimulus were utilized. A placebo effect reduced the motion sickness incidence (MSI) from 100% to 59%. Administration of dimenhydrinate reduced the MSI to 32%, and use of the transdermal therapeutic system scopolamine (TTS-scopolamine) further reduced the MSI TO 16%. TTS-scopolamine afforded 73% protection against motion-induced nausea, compared to 46% protection with dimenhydrinate. The TTS-scopolamine is designed to remain in the body for 72 hours, providing advantages over intramuscular or oral administration of scopolamine, which include reduced daily dosage, and an effective alternate to the gastrointestinal tract for administrating medication at times of gastrointestinal distress.

screening.rationale: Crossover RCT reported and quantified a placebo response (placebo reduced motion sickness incidence from 100% to 59%), so placebo response was analyzed as an object of study.

classification.summary: Compared transdermal scopolamine, oral dimenhydrinate, and placebo in a double-blind crossover and found placebo reduced motion sickness incidence from 100% to 59%, with scopolamine and dimenhydrinate providing greater protection.
classification.key_finding: Placebo reduced motion sickness incidence from 100% to 59%; scopolamine reduced MSI to 16% (73% protection) and dimenhydrinate to 32% (46% protection).

title: Nonspecific factors and side effect complaints. Factors affecting the incidence of drowsiness in drug and placebo treated anxious and depressed outpatients.
abstract: Discriminant function analyses were applied to data obtained from anxious psychiatric outpatients treated with either chlordiazepoxide (n = 353) or placebo (n = 259) and depressed outpatients treated with either amitriptyline (n = 310) or placebo (n = 328), who had participated in controlled drug trials of 4 weeks' duration, in an attempt to identify factors associated with complaints of drowsiness made by these patients. Although the magnitude of the relationships between individual predictors and drowsiness was small, several factors emerged which had consistent impact across treatment groups. Predictors of complaints of drowsiness attributed to active drugs arose primarily from demographic attributes probably reflective of life style, and from illness and treatment history. In contrast, predictors of drowsiness attributed to placebo were almost exclusively confined to indices of the severity of several aspects of presenting symptomatology. In particular, more frequent complaints of drug-induced drowsiness were found among better educated individuals with an illness of long duration. Complaints of placebo-induced drowsiness were more common among patients with more severe emotional (phobic-obsessive) symptomatology and more frequent headaches and among those individuals in whom hypochondriasis was less severe.

screening.rationale: Secondary analysis of clinical trial data that specifically examined predictors of drowsiness complaints attributed to placebo arms (i.e., placebo/nocebo responses).

classification.summary: Analyzed predictors of drowsiness complaints in anxious and depressed outpatients in drug and placebo arms of randomized trials and found placebo-attributed drowsiness was associated with greater baseline symptom severity and headache frequency.
classification.key_finding: Placebo-attributed drowsiness complaints were more common among patients with more severe phobic-obsessive symptoms and more frequent headaches, whereas drug-attributed drowsiness related more to demographic and illness/treatment history.

title: Ethics of clinical trials -- the use of placebo.

screening.rationale: Paper is a commentary on the ethics of placebo use in clinical trials, making placebo/nocebo ethics the main subject and thus eligible.

classification.summary: Discusses ethical issues and considerations surrounding the use of placebo controls in clinical trials, in light of standards such as the Declaration of Helsinki.

title: Placebo reaction in neurotics rated with the SCL-90 questionnaire.

screening.rationale: Title explicitly studies 'placebo reaction' in neurotic patients using SCL-90, indicating the placebo response was an object of study despite no abstract.

classification.summary: Studied placebo reaction in patients with neurotic disorders using the SCL-90 questionnaire.

title: Classification of placebo drugs: effect of color.
abstract: To study the role of color in the pscyhological effects of placebo drugs, 100 subjects were asked to place each of six different colored capsules into one of three classifications of drug effects. Results indicate that red and yellow placebos are classified as stimulants while blue placebos are classified as depressants.

screening.rationale: Empirical human study whose main aim was to examine placebo-related perceptions of capsule color (treatment cues), fitting placebo science inclusion criteria.

classification.summary: Found that participants classified red and yellow capsules as stimulants and blue capsules as depressants, indicating capsule color influences perceived drug effects.
classification.key_finding: Red/yellow capsules were perceived as stimulants while blue capsules were perceived as depressants.

title: Subject expectancy and the reduction of cold pressor pain with acupuncture and placebo acupuncture.

screening.rationale: Title indicates an empirical clinical trial that manipulated subject expectancy and compared acupuncture with placebo acupuncture, directly addressing placebo/expectancy effects on pain.

classification.summary: Investigated how subject expectancy influenced reduction of cold pressor pain when receiving acupuncture versus placebo acupuncture in human participants.

title: Two Bass Scale factors and response to placebo and anxiolytic drugs.
abstract: Two principal oblique factors are identified in the Bass Social Acquiescence Scale, a measure previously shown to correlate positively with placebo response and negatively with anxiolytic drug response. The two factors appeared very similar in separate analyses of data from samples of 941 psychiatric outpatients and 1,837 college students. Also, results are presented which indicate that one factor, tentatively labeled "traditionalism", accounted for the empirically observed relationships to placebo and drug response in two clinical trials.

screening.rationale: Paper empirically analyzed personality-scale factors that predicted placebo and drug responses in clinical trials, so placebo response is an object of study.

classification.summary: Analyzed Bass Social Acquiescence Scale factors across large samples and two clinical trials and found one factor ('traditionalism') accounted for relationships with placebo and anxiolytic drug response.
classification.key_finding: Found that a 'traditionalism' factor correlated positively with placebo response and negatively with anxiolytic drug response in two clinical trials.

title: Expectancy effects of labels: fact or artifact?
mesh: Education of Persons with Intellectual Disabilities

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title implies study of expectancy effects in labeled children but insufficient information to confirm placebo/nocebo relevance or methods.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title suggested an empirical study of expectancy effects of labels in children, but methods and findings were not provided.

title: The current status of placebo in hospital practice.
abstract: Despite a voluminous literature on the topic of placebo, there has been little documentation of either actual clinical practice of prescribing placebo or the attitudes that surround it. Through a questionnaire survey of all head nurses of clinical units in one health services area of Connecticut, data were obtained on current practices regarding placebo use in the natural hospital setting. Multiple reasons for placebo use in the natural hospital setting. Multiple reasons for placebo use were given, and it was noted that patients receiving placebo tended to be viewed in certain ways. The effectiveness of placebo in symptom relief was reported as nearly double that reported in the experimental literature. Methodologic issues of the study and of placebo investigation, in general, are discussed. Because common clinical problems appear to generate most instances of placebo use, several issues pertinent to medical education are raised. Some future directions for placebo research are proposed.

screening.rationale: Survey of head nurses about actual placebo prescribing practices and attitudes addresses placebo use in clinical practice (placebo science/attitudes), meeting inclusion for placebo_science_other.

classification.summary: Surveyed head nurses about placebo prescribing and attitudes in a Connecticut hospital area and reported reasons for use and perceived effectiveness, noting higher effectiveness estimates than experimental literature.
classification.key_finding: Found that nurses reported using placebos for common clinical problems and rated their effectiveness for symptom relief nearly twice that reported in experimental studies.

title: Analgesia for operative dentistry: a comparison of acupuncture and placebo.
journal: Oral surgery, oral medicine, and oral pathology
journal_abbrev: Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol
abstract: Fifty-one volunteer patients participated in a study to evaluate the effectiveness of acupuncture as an analgesic for operative dentistry. For the twenty-six patients randomly assigned to an acupuncture group, needles were inserted through specially designed holders into the Ho-Ku points, located between the first and second metacarpals. An acupuncture pulse generator provided electrical current. For the twenty-five patients in a placebo group, the identical needle and holder arrangement was used. When inserted, however, the needles became embedded in plastic on the undersurface of the holders and did not touch the skin of the patient or receive any electrical stimulation. The patients and dentists were blind to this procedural variation. Analysis of ratings and responses indicated no differences in findings for the acupuncture and placebo procedures, with both having 100% success and high levels of patient acceptance. Since there was no electric current or penetration of the skin in the placebo group, the findings suggest that the successful use of acupuncture for restorative dentistry may be due to psychological and/or placebo effects in combination with a possible diminished need for analgesia because of the modern use of the high-speed drill.

screening.rationale: Randomized sham-controlled trial of acupuncture where placebo/sham response and psychological/placebo explanations were central to the study conclusions.

classification.summary: Randomized trial compared electroacupuncture versus a nonpenetrating, nonstimulated placebo acupuncture in 51 dental patients and found no differences, with both groups showing high success rates.
classification.key_finding: Found no difference between real electroacupuncture and placebo acupuncture; both reported 100% success in analgesia.

title: Human drug self-administration: double-blind comparison of pentobarbital, diazepam, chlorpromazine and placebo.
journal: The Journal of pharmacology and experimental therapeutics

screening.rationale: Title indicates a double-blind drug self-administration trial including a placebo arm, but no abstract or full text is available to determine whether the paper analyzed placebo/nocebo effects or only used placebo as a comparator for drug reinforcement.

classification.summary: Insufficient information in the record to determine whether the study examined placebo/nocebo effects or used placebo merely as a control in a drug self-administration trial.

title: Placebo therapy. The ethical dimension.

screening.rationale: Article's title and MeSH indicate a substantive ethical discussion of placebo therapy (placebo_science_other), which meets inclusion for placebo science commentary.

classification.summary: Discussed the ethical dimensions of using placebo therapy in clinical practice, focusing on physician–patient relations and consent.

title: Knowledge and use of placebos by house officers and nurses.
abstract: Sixty house officers and 39 registered nurses in a university teaching hospital were surveyed to ascertain their knowledge of placebo action and their patterns of placebo use. The majority of physicians and nurses greatly underestimated the percentage of patients who experience pain relief when given placebo. Placebos typically were given to disliked patients who were suspected of exaggerating their pain or had failed to respond to usual medical regimens, or both. Positive responses to placebo medication were then interpreted by the physicians as evidence that the pain had no physiologic basis. Many studies have shown that overdemanding and complaining patients are, if anything, less likely to respond to placebo than patients well liked by the hospital staff. Nevertheless the results of our survey suggest that this is precisely the type of patient "at risk" for placebo treatment.

screening.rationale: Survey of clinicians' knowledge and use of placebos directly studies placebo-related attitudes and prescribing practices (placebo science: clinical use/ethics), meeting inclusion criteria for surveys of placebo prescribing/attitudes.

classification.summary: Surveyed 60 house officers and 39 nurses about placebo knowledge and use, finding misestimation of placebo analgesia and targeted placebo use for disliked or suspected-exaggerating patients.
classification.key_finding: Clinicians underestimated placebo analgesia rates and commonly gave placebos to patients perceived as exaggerating or disliked.

title: Role of pain in placebo analgesia.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
journal_abbrev: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
abstract: The hypothesis that perceived pain intensity can influence placebo analgesia was tested. One hundred and seven subjects rated their pain from from 0 to 10 on a visual analog scale after a standard wisdom tooth extraction. The expected course of such postoperative pain in the absence of therapy or placebo is a steady increase; this was confirmed by blind administration of the placebo. When placebos were given intravenously in view of the patients, some (placebo nonresponders) reported that their pain increased, whereas others (placebo responders) reported that their pain either decreased or remained the same over the next 60 min. A placebo response was more likely to occur if the pain rating 5 min prior to placebo administration (initial pain) was greater than 2.6. Furthermore, placebo responders with initial pain above this 2.6 level reported significantly greater mean analgesia than those with lower initial pain. Indeed, responders with initial pain less than 2.6 reported no change in pain during the 60 min after administration of a placebo. When their initial pain level was greater than 2.6, they reported a steady decline in pain over this period. However, above the 2.6 level there was no obvious relationship between the magnitude of the placebo analgesia and the initial pain.

screening.rationale: Empirical study that analyzed placebo (IV) arm within postoperative tooth-extraction patients and reported predictors and magnitude of placebo analgesia (placebo response).

classification.summary: Found that after IV placebo given openly following wisdom-tooth extraction, patients with initial pain >2.6 were more likely to show analgesia over the next 60 minutes than those with lower initial pain.
classification.key_finding: Placebo responders with initial pain above 2.6 reported significant analgesia over 60 minutes; responders below 2.6 showed no change.

title: Angina pectoris and the placebo effect.
journal: The New England journal of medicine

screening.rationale: Title explicitly addresses the placebo effect in angina though no abstract is available; therefore it appears to be a paper about placebo phenomena and is likely includable.

classification.summary: Discussed the placebo effect in angina pectoris in a historical/clinical context.

title: Placebo response, placebo effect, and two attributes.
abstract: Two putative predictors of placebo response were studied in three samples of psychiatric outpatients. Two groups, 73 university medical center patients and 56 college health service patients, underwent 1 week of placebo treatment. A quasi-control group of 112 patients receiving no medication waited about 1 week before beginning psychotherapy. One attribute, acquiescence or traditionalism, predicted placebo response, thereby replicating prior findings. Acquiescence was unrelated to change in controls indicating that it may represent a correlate of true placebo effect under some conditions. Additional findings suggested qualifications as to the generality of the relationship. The second attribute, autonomic awareness, was associated with change in all three samples. It appeared to predict nonspecific improvement unrelated to placebo probably due to its relationship to intensity of somatization.

screening.rationale: Empirical study that explicitly analyzed predictors of placebo response in psychiatric outpatients, comparing placebo-treated groups with a no-medication quasi-control.

classification.summary: Studied predictors of placebo response in psychiatric outpatients and found acquiescence predicted placebo response while autonomic awareness predicted nonspecific improvement across samples.
classification.key_finding: Acquiescence (traditionalism) predicted placebo-related improvement; autonomic awareness predicted improvement in both placebo and control groups, suggesting nonspecific somatization-related change.

title: The placebo and its role in clinical pharmacology.
journal: Methods and findings in experimental and clinical pharmacology
abstract: This paper reviews literature concerning the placebo with respect to its true meaning, and possible modes of action. It also considers the type of person most likely to respond to the placebo effect. These factors are then discussed with a particular emphasis being put on the significance of the placebo in clinical pharmacological studies.

screening.rationale: Narrative review whose stated aim was to examine the meaning, mechanisms, responder characteristics, and significance of the placebo in clinical pharmacology, so placebo is the main subject.

classification.summary: Reviews definitions, possible mechanisms, responder characteristics, and the significance of the placebo in clinical pharmacology.

title: Acupuncture as a placebo.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title implies discussion of acupuncture as a placebo but insufficient information to determine whether the paper reports empirical data or is a commentary/review.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title suggested the paper discussed acupuncture in the context of placebo but full content was not available to judge study type or findings.

title: O'Leary and Borkovec's conceptualization of placebo: the placebo paradox.

screening.rationale: Paper is a conceptual/commentary focused on placebo conceptualization in psychotherapy (placebo science broader), meeting inclusion criterion for placebo science work.

classification.summary: Commentary critiqued O'Leary and Borkovec's conceptualization of placebo in psychotherapy and discussed the 'placebo paradox'.

title: The effect of placebo and tricyclic antidepressants on cortical evoked potentials in depressed patients.
abstract: Cortical evoked potentials in depressives were recorded in order to study stimulus intensity control in this group, and also to study the effect of treatment. In a sample of 33 psychiatric patients, the amplitudes of visual and auditory evoked potentials were found to be significantly greater during depression, than at recovery. The changes which appeared to be due to recovery were found not only in patients treated with tricyclic antidepressants (n = 22), but in those who had recovered following treatment with placebo (n = 11). The changes were most evident in the auditory system. In addition, no diagnostic predictors differentiated depressed patients who subsequently recovered on placebo from those who did not. It is concluded that: (i) cortical evoked potentials may change in amplitude with emotional state; (ii) placebo may have physiological consequences usually attributed to drugs alone.

screening.rationale: Clinical trial explicitly analyzed physiological and clinical changes in patients who recovered on placebo, so placebo response was an object of study.

classification.summary: Tested depressed patients before and after treatment and found auditory and visual evoked potential amplitudes decreased with recovery in both tricyclic-treated and placebo-treated patients.
classification.key_finding: Found that cortical evoked potential amplitudes decreased with recovery and that similar physiological changes occurred in patients who recovered on placebo (n=11), indicating placebo-linked physiological effects.

title: EEG sleep in primary depression. A longitudinal placebo study.
abstract: Characteristic EEG sleep changes in depression are highlighted by a sleep continuity disturbance, delta sleep reduction, and a shortened REM latency. Since these findings have been derived primarily from only a few baseline recordings, questions regarding their persistence and/or variability have not been previously addressed. As part of an extensive set of investigations of EEG sleep in depression, we examined nightly the sleep of 12 hospitalized, non-delusional, primary depressives who were involved in a program of active psychosocial treatment intervention and received only placebo during a 5-week study period. EEG sleep findings revealed a relative lack of change across time, particularly in those parameters reported to be associated with a primary or 'biologic' depressive episode. While some degree of clinical improvement was noted, the group failed to achieve a state of remission or even partial remission as determined by the Hamilton Rating Scale. It appears that the major sleep alterations associated with such disorders persist for up to at least 5 weeks in the absence of pharmacologic or other somatic intervention.

screening.rationale: Empirical longitudinal study of depressed patients receiving only placebo that analyzed placebo-arm changes in EEG sleep and clinical measures (single-group pre-post placebo response).

classification.summary: Followed 12 hospitalized patients with primary depression who received only placebo during five weeks and found persistent EEG sleep abnormalities with only modest clinical improvement.
classification.key_finding: Found no appreciable change in EEG sleep abnormalities (reduced delta sleep, shortened REM latency) over 5 weeks despite some clinical symptom improvement without remission.

title: The pleasing placebo.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text available and bibliographic info (title and MeSH 'Placebos') is insufficient to judge whether the article studies placebo phenomena or is a commentary/editorial.

classification.summary: No abstract or full text was available; bibliographic entry titled 'The pleasing placebo' (American Pharmacy, 1979) mentioned placebos but did not provide sufficient information to determine study aims or design.

title: Double-blind trial of the use of transfer factor in the treatment of Crohn's disease.
abstract: We have undertaken a double-blind controlled trial of the use of transfer factor in Crohn's disease. Thirty-three patients with known Crohn's disease completed the trial in which half the patients had three injections of transfer factor and the other half were given saline. After six months there was no significant difference in the clinical condition of either of the two groups compared with before receiving treatment. There was also no difference in their in vitro lymphocyte function, although a number of patients exhibited altered responsiveness to skin testing with tuberculin or streptokinase/streptodornase. A signficant fall on Crohn's disease activity index score occurred over the initial 'acclimatising period' before the trial was started, probably related to overcoming initial introspection and the placebo effect of being part of a trial.

screening.rationale: Although primarily an efficacy RCT, the paper reported and analyzed a pre-trial clinical improvement attributed to a placebo effect, making placebo response an object of study.

classification.summary: Conducted a double-blind RCT of transfer factor versus saline in Crohn's disease (n=33) and found no treatment effect, but observed a significant pre-trial fall in disease activity attributed to a placebo/acclimatisation effect.
classification.key_finding: No difference between transfer factor and saline; significant decrease in Crohn's Disease Activity Index during pre-trial acclimatisation, consistent with a placebo response.

title: Ménière's disease: lithium treatment (demonstration of placebo effect in a doubleblind cross-over trial).

screening.rationale: Title reports a double-blind cross-over trial explicitly demonstrating a placebo effect in lithium treatment for Menière's disease, indicating placebo was the study object.

classification.summary: Reported a double-blind crossover trial in Menière's disease that demonstrated a placebo effect during lithium treatment.
classification.key_finding: Found a placebo effect in the double-blind crossover trial comparing lithium and placebo.

title: Double-blind and triple-blind assessments of medication and placebo responses in hyperactive children.
abstract: Hyperactive boys taking psychostimulant medication were studied using a randomized, placebo-controlled, crossover design. Behavior ratings and medication guesstimates were obtained for the boys when they were given methylphenidate (Ritalin) and when they were given a placebo. The ratings showed positive medication-related changes, and the guesses, done by independent judges, were significantly better than chance. The pattern of ratings for double-blind and triple-blind raters was identical. These results imply that positive psychostimulant effects are not attributable to rater sensitization or expectancy. The medication-placebo differences were highly reliable for the group comparisons and were in the predicted direction for 21 of 22 individuals, but the magnitude of the change for many individuals was not dramatic. Implications for child psychopharmacology research and differences between clinical and experimental significance are discussed.

screening.rationale: Randomized placebo-controlled crossover trial included substantial analysis of blinding/expectancy (trial methodology) bearing on placebo-related bias rather than solely testing drug efficacy.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind crossover trial of methylphenidate versus placebo in hyperactive boys analyzed behavior ratings and rater guesses, and found medication effects were reliable while rater guesses exceeded chance, arguing against rater-expectancy bias.
classification.key_finding: Medication-placebo differences were highly reliable for group comparisons and were in the predicted direction for 21 of 22 individuals, indicating effects were not attributable to rater expectancy.

title: The use of placebo and deception.

screening.rationale: Title and MeSH terms indicate the paper's primary focus is ethical issues of placebo use and deception, meeting the 'placebo science other' inclusion criterion.

classification.summary: Discusses ethical issues around the use of placebos and deception in human research, including informed consent and risk assessment.

title: The efficacy of intra-articularly administered MYC 2095, triamcinolone hexacetonide and placebo in gonarthritis. A combined double-blind clinical trial.
abstract: We report the results of a double-blind three-centre study, employing a cross-over design, set up to compare the efficacy of intra-articular injections of Myc 2095 (20 mg), triamcinolone hexacetonide (Lederspan) (20 mg) and placebo in 40 patients with synovitis of the knee joint. Each patient included in the study contributed data on 2 of the 3 treatment variables being compared. Seven clinical parameters were assessed every 6 weeks, while the doctor's and the patient's assessments were scored. Intra articular treatment both with Myc 2095 and triamcinolone hexacetonide proved to be effective. Placebo response was also very high. After the first Myc 2095 injection, improvement in "tenderness", "pain under load" and "swelling and hydrops" was significantly superior to that following placebo treatment. The evaluation of the second injections indicated a marked carry-over effect from the first course. This was also evident from the doctor's and patient's assessments. The importance of including a placebo in the evaluation of anti-phlogistic drugs in clinical trials, emerged from this study.

screening.rationale: Randomized double-blind crossover trial analyzed placebo responses and compared active intra-articular treatments versus placebo, explicitly reporting high placebo response and carry-over effects.

classification.summary: Reported a double-blind crossover RCT in 40 patients with knee synovitis where two active intra-articular steroids outperformed placebo on several outcomes, but placebo responses were also high and carry-over effects were noted.
classification.key_finding: Found high placebo response; after the first injection, Myc 2095 produced significantly greater improvement than placebo on tenderness, pain on load, and swelling.

title: Effect of acetylsalicylic acid, paracetamol and placebo on pain and blood loss in dysmenorrheic women.
journal: Acta obstetricia et gynecologica Scandinavica. Supplement
abstract: The analgesic effect of paracetamol, acetyl-salicylic acid, and placebo on dysmenorrhea were compared in a double-blind cross-over study of 30 women. There was a moderate placebo effect, but no significant difference was found between the three treatments. Blood loss was also measured and it did not vary, with the type of drug ingested. It is concluded that paracetamol and acetylsalicylic acid in the doses used (0.5 g x 4 for 3 days) were not effective against heavy dysmenorrhea, and that none of the drugs influenced the amount of blood lost.

screening.rationale: Double-blind crossover trial reported a measurable placebo (within-arm) analgesic response and analyzed placebo alongside active drugs, so placebo response was an object of study.

classification.summary: Compared aspirin, paracetamol, and placebo in a double-blind crossover of 30 women with dysmenorrhea and found a moderate placebo analgesic response but no difference between treatments or effect on menstrual blood loss.
classification.key_finding: Found a moderate placebo-related reduction in pain (subjective) but no treatment differences and no change in measured blood loss.

title: Handwriting deficits in children with minimal brain dysfunction: effects of methylphenidate (Ritalin) and placebo.

screening.rationale: No abstract or full text provided; title indicates a comparison of methylphenidate and placebo for handwriting in children but it's unclear whether placebo/placebo response was analyzed as an object of study versus serving only as a control for drug efficacy.

classification.summary: Compared methylphenidate versus placebo on handwriting deficits in children with minimal brain dysfunction; abstract unavailable so role of placebo as object of study was unclear.

title: A critical evaluation of the glycerol test in Meniere's disease.
abstract: From the literature it is apparent that the glycerol test is being used frequently to evaluate Meniere patients, with regard to the choice of treatment, and in particular to find those who are suitable for surgery with different decompressive procedures. In our previous investigations on such patients we found that they often are extremely good placebo responders and it was natural to evaluate how important such psychological factors would be for the outcome of the glycerol test. In a group of patients with typical objective and subjective symptoms of Meniere's disease, the glycerol test was applied twice to each patient. In one of the tests, the patient was told that we would expect hearing to improve. In the other test, where the actual amount of glycerol was the same, we had the solution prepared with a different taste, and the patient was informed that we now would expect the hearing to deteriorate. The sequence of the two tests was randomly chosen for each patient. Most frequently the patient would follow our instructions, i.e. obtained a poorer hearing threshold when instructed to, and vice versa. The results are discussed with a special view to the risk of selection of suggestion-sensitive patients by this test.

screening.rationale: Within-subject randomized manipulation of expectation about the glycerol test examined suggestion/placebo effects on hearing, so placebo/nocebo context was the study's object.

classification.summary: Randomized within-subject study in Meniere patients manipulated verbal expectation (improve vs deteriorate) across identical glycerol tests and found hearing changes concordant with instructions, suggesting strong suggestion effects.
classification.key_finding: Most patients' hearing thresholds changed in the direction of the verbal suggestion despite identical glycerol dosing, indicating suggestion-driven effects on the glycerol test.

title: A prospective, controlled trial of six forms of hormone replacement therapy given to postmenopausal women.
journal: British journal of obstetrics and gynaecology
abstract: This study was undertaken to investigate the effect of various forms of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) upon postmenopausal women while controlling as many variables as possible. It was felt that the age, duration of amenorrhoea and the general health of the patients should be as comparable as possible and that each patient should provide her own pretherapy and post-therapy control data. In addition, it was felt that any placebo effect should be investigated and the patients were therefore randomly allocated to placebo tablets or one of six available forms of HRT. The age/sex registers of two large general practices were scrutinized and all women between 49 and 54 years of age were asked to cooperate; for a variety of reasons only 56 women were suitable and willing to take part in the project, yielding 8 women for each of the seven possible therapy groups. Blood samples were taken at 7-day intervals three times before therapy was given and the mean of the three values was used as the control value. The women returned on day 21 of each subsequent therapy cycle for six consecutive months and finally three months after discontinuing therapy. From the data the following broad conclusions can be drawn: (i) some women have classic symptoms of hot flushes and sweating despite high endogenous oestrogen concentrations; (ii) vaginal cytology is a relatively poor indicator of endogenous oestrogen status; (iii) while follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) concentrations are reduced on HRT neither is decreased to anywhere near premenopausal values while prolactin is unaffected; (iv) plasma cholesterol levels are reduced on HRT, the pulse rate is slower and both systolic and diastolic blood pressure are reduced to a small but significant extent; (v) there is no adverse effect upon blood clotting; and (vi) most women experience significant or complete relief of symptoms on all forms of HRT as do some women taking a placebo. The combined preparations containing an oestrogen and progestogen produced vaginal bleeding in only 80 per cent of the women. Thus protection by regular endometrical shedding may not be afforded to all women. As vaginal bleeding is unacceptable to most women if they can achieve the same symptomatic relief without inducing menstruation, it is suggested that women have a low dose oestrogen preparation prescribed cyclically for 6 to 12 months. If therapy is to be maintained for a longer time, uterine curretage should be undertaken at regular intervals to exclude the possibility of endometrial carcinoma developing.

screening.rationale: Randomized controlled trial explicitly randomized a placebo arm and reported placebo arm symptom relief, so placebo response was an object of study.

classification.summary: Randomized trial compared six hormone replacement regimens plus placebo in postmenopausal women and found symptom relief on active HRT and in some placebo recipients, with HRT reducing lipids, pulse and blood pressure and altering gonadotropins.
classification.key_finding: Most HRT forms produced significant symptomatic relief and physiological changes, and some women randomized to placebo also reported significant or complete symptom relief.

title: Evaluation of the effects of clobazam, A 1,5 benzodiazepine, on mood and psychomotor performance in clinically anxious patients in general practice.
abstract: 1 The methodology of clinical trails of anxiolytic drugs carried out in general practice conditions is discussed. Particular problems include: the selection of suitable patients; placebo effects; the influence of non-specific variables such as life-events; and patient compliance. 2 Clobazam, a novel 1,5 benzodiazepine, and diazepam were compared with placebo in a double-blind group comparative trial in general practice, which was designed to avoid as many confounding variables as possible. Anxiety-reducing effects were evaluated and at the same time the effects of the drugs on psychomotor performance were examined. 3 Both clobazam and diazepam produced significant improvements in anxiety ratings on the Hamilton Anxiety Scale and the Morbid Anxiety Inventory, whereas placebo did not. 4 The placebo group demonstrated a significant improvement in performance on a pursuit rotor and digit symbol substitution test (DSST), whereas the diazepam group's performance did not change. The clobazam group showed improvement in both tests, significantly so in the DSST. This suggests that diazepam produces impairment in performance, which had negated the practice effects seen in the placebo group, whereas clobazam did not seem to produce similar impairment.

screening.rationale: Randomized controlled trial reported and analyzed placebo-arm changes (significant improvement on psychomotor tests), so placebo response was a substantive object of analysis.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind trial compared clobazam, diazepam, and placebo in anxious primary-care patients and reported that drugs reduced anxiety while the placebo group showed significant improvement on psychomotor performance tests.
classification.key_finding: Placebo group showed significant practice-related improvement on pursuit rotor and DSST despite no anxiety reduction; drugs reduced anxiety ratings.

title: The reliability and validity of a placebo test.

screening.rationale: No abstract or detail available and the title suggests a psychometric study of a 'placebo test' but it's unclear whether the paper empirically studies placebo/nocebo effects/responses or merely validates a questionnaire/measure.

classification.summary: No abstract available; title suggests a reliability and validity study of a 'placebo test' but aims and methods were not reported in the available record.

title: Clonidine in the treatment of menopausal symptoms.
journal: International journal of gynaecology and obstetrics: the official organ of the International Federation of Gynaecology and Obstetrics
abstract: Thirty-seven women complaining of hot flushes, sweating and other menopausal symptoms were treated with clonidine. A double-blind crossover trial with placebo controls was undertaken. The clonidine dose was 2 X 0.025 mg/24 hours-0.075 mg/24 hours, increased if necessary at intervals of two weeks. The effect of clonidine did not differ significantly from placebo effect in the treatment of the symptoms. Side effects during clonidine management were slight and no difference was seen in their incidence compared with that in the patients treated with the placebo. A definitive placebo response was perceivable in the decreasing of symptoms.

screening.rationale: Double-blind crossover RCT reported no drug benefit and explicitly described a measurable placebo response, so the placebo response was an object of analysis.

classification.summary: Randomized double-blind crossover trial in 37 menopausal women found clonidine was not superior to placebo and observed a clear placebo-related reduction in symptoms.
classification.key_finding: Clonidine did not differ significantly from placebo; significant symptom reduction occurred on placebo (placebo response).
